RESOLVE: Language-Agnostic Validation of GPU Kernels Through Testing, Reduction, and Proof

Ashkan Vedadi Gargary Affiliation: University of California, Riverside, Riverside, California, USA , Guido Martínez Affiliation: Math, Inc., New York City, New York, USA , Sebastian Burckhardt Affiliation: Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, USA , Gabriel Ebner Affiliation: Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, USA , Abhinav Jangda Affiliation: Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, USA , Madan Musuvathi Affiliation: Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, USA and Tyler Sorensen Affiliation: Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, USA
© none
Abstract.

AI systems can now write and optimize production GPU kernels, but validating them remains an important challenge. Evaluating the kernel on a few random inputs and checking that its outputs match a trusted reference kernel within numeric tolerances is not sufficient: races can cause nondeterministic behavior that fails to manifest in tests, and numeric tolerances can hide bugs and cause false positives even after extensive calibration.

To address this challenge, we present RESOLVE, which combines testing and formal verification to build a comprehensive kernel validation pipeline. It operates in three steps: First, it tests for nondeterminism using binary instrumentation that perturbs execution timing to expose races. Second, an agent rewrites the candidate and reference kernels to obtain "reduced-concurrency" versions that are simpler to analyze but still produce bitwise-identical outputs in all tests. Third, the reduced kernels are formally analyzed in the F*/Pulse framework and prove that they perform the same computation on real numbers. This sidesteps the need for numeric tolerances. We show that RESOLVE can validate a broad selection of kernels using KernelBench, and prove equivalence across fused GEMMs in three state-of-the-art frameworks and languages: CUTLASS, Triton, and Gluon. It also analyzes mega-kernels, notoriously difficult to validate, and finds four previously unreported issues, including two clear bugs. We show that agents can use RESOLVE to repair the issues, with minimal performance impact, highlighting that agents can optimize aggressively when they can rigorously check their results.

1. Introduction

GPU kernels determine much of the performance of modern AI workloads. Recent systems have shown that AI agents can generate and optimize these kernels (Ouyang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), producing candidates far faster than humans can review them for correctness. Kernel generation is therefore creating a new validation bottleneck: an optimization that cannot be trusted cannot safely be deployed, regardless of its speed.

The predominant method for validating GPU kernels is reference-based testing (Ouyang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025): execute a candidate and a trusted reference on representative inputs and compare their outputs. This approach is often effective for machine-learning kernels, whose behavior is determined largely by tensor shapes, data types, layouts, and other discrete configurations that can be sampled systematically. Nevertheless, two challenges remain even with broad input coverage.

First, concurrency bugs may manifest only under rare thread or warp schedules and therefore remain hidden across repeated executions. Second, valid optimizations may reorder floating-point operations and produce outputs that are not bitwise identical to the reference. Testing must consequently compare outputs using a numerical tolerance, but a permissive tolerance can conceal bugs while a restrictive one can reject valid optimizations.

Formal verification can instead establish equivalence for all inputs covered by a specification (Martínez et al., 2026; Chatterjee et al., 2026). Its applicability, however, is limited by the verifier’s semantic coverage. Modern kernels rely on warp intrinsics, asynchronous memory operations, tensor-core instructions, and synchronization patterns that existing verification frameworks do not fully model. Because GPU programming models and hardware features evolve faster than their formalizations, directly verifying optimized production kernels remains impractical.

This paper presents RESOLVE, a GPU-kernel validation framework that bridges the gap between the broad applicability of testing and the rigorous guarantees of formal verification. RESOLVE’s central idea is to separate concurrency correctness from functional correctness, and to use a different validation technique for each. This decomposition exploits a key property of machine-learning kernels: they are generally intended to be deterministic, producing the same output for a given input regardless of thread schedule. This allows RESOLVE to focus on capturing a broad set of concurrency issues as schedule-dependent nondeterminism, while deferring functional equivalence to a formal proof.

Given a candidate kernel CC and a trusted reference kernel RR, RESOLVE asks agents to generate reduced-concurrency kernels CrC_{r} and RrR_{r}. These reductions remove asynchronous pipelines, synchronization, and other concurrency constructs that impede formal reasoning, while seeking to preserve the bitwise behavior of their respective originals. Thus, CC and RR may use complex concurrency patterns and recent hardware features, while CrC_{r} and RrR_{r} are designed to fall within the semantic coverage of the verifier.

RESOLVE validates concurrency correctness using systematic concurrency testing (Burckhardt et al., 2010; Stephenson et al., 2026). Using the NVBit binary-instrumentation framework (Villa et al., 2019), RESOLVE perturbs the timing of scheduling-relevant operations to explore different schedules. A lightweight memory analysis focuses these perturbations on GPU scopes and memory regions in which conflicting accesses may occur. As this analysis operates on the compiled NVIDIA GPU binary, it is independent of the source language or framework used to generate the kernel, including CUDA, Triton (Tillet et al., 2019), Gluon (Triton Contributors, 2026), and CUTLASS (NVIDIA, 2023).

RESOLVE then compares executions bit-for-bit. For a fixed input, repeated executions of each kernel must produce identical results, and each reduced kernel must produce the same result as its original. These comparisons distinguish two failure modes. If repeated executions of the same kernel differ, RESOLVE reports schedule-dependent behavior. If an original and its reduced kernel are individually deterministic but differ from one another, RESOLVE rejects the reduction and asks the agent to try again. At these boundaries, bitwise comparison provides an exact per-execution oracle and requires no numerical tolerance.

To verify functional correctness, agents translate CrC_{r} and RrR_{r} into Kuiper (Martínez et al., 2026) kernels CkC_{k} and RkR_{k}, respectively. Kuiper is a verification language built on the F*/Pulse concurrent separation logic (Ebner et al., 2025) that covers a subset of CUDA and compiles to it. RESOLVE checks the correspondence between each Kuiper translation and its reduced executable using bitwise testing. Agents then construct an algebraic specification from the trusted reference alone and prove in Kuiper that both CkC_{k} and RkR_{k} satisfy it. Because the specification is derived without consulting the candidate, the candidate cannot influence the criterion against which it is judged. A successful proof establishes that CkC_{k} and RkR_{k} implement the same algebraic computation, even when valid floating-point reorderings cause them to produce numerically different results.

RESOLVE therefore uses testing where bitwise equality provides an exact per-execution oracle and formal verification where numerical testing requires an approximate one. Testing connects optimized binaries to proof-friendly representations, extending formal reasoning to kernels that use languages and hardware features outside the verifier’s semantic coverage. Agents construct the reductions, translations, specifications, and proofs, but do not serve as correctness oracles: their outputs must pass bitwise testing or formal proof checking.

We evaluate RESOLVE on KernelBench kernels, complex state-of-the-art fused GEMM kernels written using Triton, Gluon, and CUTLASS, and three mega-kernels. Although every KernelBench candidate had passed the benchmark’s existing tolerance-based tests, RESOLVE identified two incorrect candidates. We also design a mutation testing strategy to evaluate how effectively our concurrency testing finds synchronization faults. The fused GEMMs in particular use concurrency and hardware features outside Kuiper’s directly supported subset, and RESOLVE validated them regardless, demonstrating that reduction can extend formal reasoning to kernels that cannot be verified directly. Across the mega-kernels, RESOLVE found four previously unreported issues, including two clear bugs. Agents repaired them, and RESOLVE tested the repairs, which changed performance by less than 2% on three of the four.

Contributions.

In summary, we present RESOLVE, a workflow to validate GPU kernels. It consists of:

  1. (1)

    Efficient binary-level determinism testing (§3): timing perturbation on SASS, needing no source or compiler and covering any language or library.

  2. (2)

    Bitwise concurrency reduction (§4): an agent rewrites both programs with as little concurrency as possible, accepted only when the output is bitwise equivalent.

  3. (3)

    Automated equivalence proof (§5): agents write a specification from the trusted reference alone and a program for each side satisfying it, so an optimization can differ bitwise and still be accepted.

  4. (4)

    Evaluation (§6.2): sampled KernelBench kernels, state-of-the-art fused GEMMs in Triton, Gluon, and CUTLASS, and three mega-kernels, in which we find four unreported issues.

Given those reports, agents repaired the bugs, four with verified deterministic fixes, showing that better testing tools can make agentic kernel optimization more ambitious.

2. GPU Background and Setup

A GPU is built from many simple cores and gets its performance from running enormous numbers of threads. Recent GPUs also have fixed-function tensor cores that perform a small matrix multiply in a single instruction. A GPU function is called a kernel, and many thousands of threads run it at once. Threads are grouped into warps of 32 that advance together, warps into cooperative thread arrays (CTAs, also called blocks) whose threads share a fast on-chip scratchpad, and CTAs into a grid that covers the device. The newest hardware adds a cluster level between the CTA and the grid. Memory follows the same levels: each thread has private registers, each CTA has shared memory that only its own threads can reach, and every thread can reach a large global memory. Launching a kernel runs one grid to completion.

Most kernels are still written in CUDA, but a lot of performance work now happens in languages above it. Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) lets a kernel be written over tiles and leaves the compiler to assign work to threads and to place data in shared memory. Gluon (Triton Contributors, 2026) sits on the same compiler but exposes layouts, memory movement and asynchrony, so the programmer controls what Triton decides. CUTLASS (NVIDIA, 2023) is a C++ template library of hand-tuned building blocks for matrix multiply and its epilogues. Vendor libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN ship as binaries, with no source or PTX to inspect. The only common foundation is SASS, the relatively undocumented binary code for NVIDIA GPUs, unique to each architecture.

Kernels have been getting larger. A single operation is usually limited by memory rather than arithmetic: it reads its inputs from global memory, computes, and writes the result back for the next operation to read again. Fusing several operations into one kernel removes those round trips. Fusion used to mean a matrix multiply with an activation attached to it. Now it means the whole MLP block of §6.3, the multi-layer perceptron that follows attention in every transformer layer of a modern LLM, or the mega-kernels of §6.4, which put an entire model in one launch. Two of those mega-kernels implement a mixture of experts, which replaces the MLP block with many copies of it and routes each token to a few.

Fusing more work into one kernel puts more concurrency in it, and spreads that concurrency across more scopes. This paper is concerned with races: memory conflicts, at least one of them a write, unordered by synchronization. A race gives a different outcome depending on the scheduler. Races can occur at every level of the hierarchy, and each level has its own way of ordering accesses: threads in a warp advance together, threads in a CTA can be ordered with __syncthreads(), and separate CTAs need a grid-wide barrier or atomics. The memory scopes match, so shared memory can only be raced on from inside one CTA and global memory from anywhere. Asynchronous copies and TMA transfers add another boundary, between issuing a transfer and the point at which its result is safe to read.

Reasoning about GPU programs almost always requires reasoning about floating-point computation, which does not behave like real arithmetic. Addition is not associative, so summing the same values in a different order changes the last bits, and any kernel that splits a reduction across threads is choosing an order. Fast-math flags widen the gap by letting the compiler reassociate, contract a multiply and an add into one fused operation, and replace a division by a reciprocal. Transcendental functions have no exact implementation, so an exponential ends up as a polynomial or a Taylor series, and two kernels can choose different ones. Tensor cores accumulate in their own precision and their own order, so a matrix multiply run on them does not agree bit for bit with the same multiply built out of ordinary fused multiply-adds. Two kernels that compute the same mathematical function may not produce the same bits.

The kernels in this paper are tensor kernels, and we assume their shapes are fixed. ML kernels are tuned, and often recompiled, for the shapes they will actually see, so this is how they are written anyway. It also makes our testing tractable: with the shapes fixed, a kernel issues a fixed number of memory accesses, so it can be traced in full and replayed on the same input under many schedules.

2.1. RESOLVE Kernel Bench and Kernel Executors

Throughout this work we need kernels to evaluate, and we draw on several corpora. For breadth and characterization we built one, the RESOLVE Kernel Bench (RKB), which pairs each of the 100 KernelBench Level 1 kernels (Ouyang et al., 2025) with an optimized candidate. We generated the candidates with GPT-5.6 Sol and retried until each compiled and passed the tolerance tests shipped with the benchmark, so every candidate has already passed a conventional tolerance oracle.

RESOLVE assumes each kernel comes with a kernel executor. It runs the kernel a fixed number of times and hashes all of memory after each run, not just the output. That hash is what every comparison in RESOLVE is made on, between two runs of the same kernel and between a kernel and its reduced program. Hashing is only a way to save space: the comparisons are all equality tests, so we never need to keep a full copy of memory from every run.

Inputs are tensors drawn from ten families of distributions, chosen per operation and seeded so a run can be replayed on the same input and any difference between runs is a property of the kernel. Uniform random data can miss branches and leave corner cases of floating-point arithmetic unexercised, so the families are built to cover both: degenerate, sparse and sentinel values, awkward magnitudes and cancellation, quantization boundaries, and the ties, indices, masks and lengths that steer control flow. We give their definitions in the artifact. Every kernel is run a fixed number of times on each input.

3. Testing for Determinism

RESOLVE requires the kernels it validates to be deterministic: on a given input, a kernel must produce the same output on every run. The determinism tester checks this, treating the kernel as a black box. Requiring determinism has two big advantages. First, it enables and improves the rest of our reduction pipeline, by simplifying subsequent reductions and boosting the effectiveness of random testing. Second, it can flag synchronization errors in kernels. For example, a mistakenly omitted barrier can cause nondeterminism.

Requiring determinism also has a potential disadvantage: we may reject kernels that are non-deterministic and yet correct (legitimate nondeterminism). For example, a kernel may intentionally use a nondeterministic reduction order (say, based on atomicAdd), leading to slightly different results due to the non-associativity of floating-point addition.

Empirically, legitimate nondeterminism is rare for GPU kernels. Only one of the 100 kernels in RKB uses a floating-point atomicAdd; the rest appeared deterministic on inspection and under testing (§6.2), so the benefits outweigh the disadvantage.

Determinism vs. Race-Freedom

The two often occur in tandem, but they are defined differently and neither implies the other. Data races are violations of synchronization rules agreed upon by a community, and there are many definitions rather than one universally accepted one. Evidence for a data race must include execution-internal details to show the violation. Nondeterminism is externally observable, and two executions that produce a different output on the same input suffice as evidence.

3.1. Characterization

RESOLVE looks for races by delaying memory operations and comparing the kernel’s full output bitwise against an unperturbed run. Delaying an access that races with another changes which of the two lands first, and the kernel can produce a different result. SuperCollider (Stephenson et al., 2026) applies the same idea to individual memory accesses, which it reaches through a compiler pass.

The difficulty is knowing where to delay: a GPU kernel runs enormous numbers of threads over large tensors, and delaying at random took hours per kernel in our pilot runs. Conflicting memory accesses are not spread evenly, though: whole memory regions and levels of the thread hierarchy may admit none at all. Since determinism bugs do not occur without conflicts, there is no point in testing such accesses. RESOLVE therefore measures the kernel in three passes over the binary, counting, tracing, and perturbation (Figure 1), placing delays only where the trace shows a conflict is possible. This brings the median time to test a kernel in RKB down to 88 seconds (§6.2).

How much memory traffic is there?

Tracing memory accesses requires a buffer, and that buffer has to be sized before the kernel runs, either to fit in memory or to keep the later analysis tractable. The first pass therefore runs the kernel under NVBit (NVIDIA’s binary instrumentation tool) and counts how many memory accesses each CTA (cooperative thread array) performs, along with the grid shape and the number of TMA (tensor memory accelerator) descriptors. Because nothing is written to the buffer and no analysis runs, the cost is instrumentation and counting alone. CTAs are sampled at random, so that later analysis is not biased toward the blocks with the lowest identifiers.

Figure 2 shows the distribution of memory-reference operand events per problem across RKB. Activity spans roughly four orders of magnitude: most problems fall between 10810^{8} and 101010^{10}, while the largest reach beyond 101110^{11}. Two problems, P31 and P32, count zero memory-reference operands and are excluded from the figure; §6.2 returns to them. These counts let RESOLVE scope the trace buffer and the analysis to each kernel, instead of over-provisioning for one that needs little or failing on one that needs more than expected. They also make explicit what any later sampling leaves out.

Where can a conflict be?

The second pass records the memory accesses themselves, including each address and the thread that issued it. From this trace RESOLVE identifies potential conflicts: pairs of accesses whose byte ranges overlap where at least one is a write. Each potential conflict is located on two axes, the memory hierarchy, global or shared, and the thread hierarchy, within a warp, within a CTA, or across CTAs. Asynchronous copies and TMA transfers are traced as well, with each descriptor decoded into the byte ranges it moves. When counting showed more accesses than the buffer can hold, RESOLVE samples whole CTAs at random rather than individual accesses, so that potential conflicts inside a CTA are still visible. How many CTAs to sample is a configuration knob. A few are usually enough, because most CTAs compute the same thing on different tiles of data, though at least two are needed to see a conflict between CTAs. This is what tells RESOLVE where to place delays and at which scope.

Figure 3 is a histogram of where potential conflicts occur across RKB. In 41 of the 100 kernels the trace found no potential conflict anywhere. Those kernels need no perturbation testing at all and are dropped from the campaign before it starts. The remaining 59 all have one in shared memory between threads of the same block, making that the scope most testing has to cover. Only 8 also have one in global memory across blocks. That small number is not a reason to skip the scope: all four of the issues we found in the mega-kernels of §6.4 are at exactly this scope. It is a reason to trace every kernel rather than assume a profile, so that testing targets the scopes that kernel actually has.

No potential conflict is reported as a bug. RESOLVE computes no happens-before relation, so a properly synchronized pair looks the same as an unsynchronized one. A potential conflict is only a place to put a delay. Unlike a static race detector, RESOLVE reports nothing unless the delay changes the output.

Does the schedule change the output?

The third pass inserts the delays: NVBit places a call before a selected memory instruction, and that call stalls the issuing thread for up to a set number of cycles, with a configured probability so that not every execution is delayed.

Perturbing a schedule to expose a concurrency bug is an old idea, and the search has to be bounded somehow: by systematic exploration (Musuvathi et al., 2008), by randomized scheduling with a probabilistic guarantee (Burckhardt et al., 2010), by directing it at reported races (Sen, 2008), or on GPUs by bounding the number of delays and directing them at conflicting atomics (Chiang et al., 2013). We bound ours by scope, using the trace to decide where a delay could matter, which keeps the binary as the only thing we need.

RESOLVE is configured with a memory region, global or shared, and a scope, and delays only the instructions the trace placed there. An inter-block delay derives the stall from the CTA index; an intra-block delay derives it from the warp identifier. A conflict across CTAs is exposed by separating CTAs, not by reordering warps inside one. How many CTAs to perturb is a configuration knob here too. The cycle count and probability are parameters we fixed rather than results. Surprisingly, neither mattered: §6.2 shows detection did not change across the ranges we swept.

RESOLVE compares the perturbed runs against an unperturbed baseline, byte for byte on the same input, stops at the first difference, and reports that difference and nothing else. Turning it into a root cause is separate work. In §6.4 agents did that from these reports, and each proposed fix was validated by running the same test again.

Limitations.

RESOLVE does not perturb every scope, and the gaps follow from working at the binary level. We have no way to slow an asynchronous load through what NVBit exposes. We attempted to perturb intra-warp races and could not: every instrumentation site is bracketed by BSSY and BSYNC, the SASS instructions that synchronize and reconverge warp control flow, so the independent thread scheduler never gets the chance to interleave differently. Conflicts between CTAs that are never resident at the same time are also out of reach; SuperCollider shuffles block identifiers to bring such pairs together, which needs compiler access that we do not want to require. A clean campaign is not a proof of race freedom, but surviving it is strong, language-agnostic, black-box evidence that the kernel computes a deterministic function, which is what the rest of RESOLVE needs.

4. Reduction

Concurrency, more than size, is what puts a fully optimized GPU kernel out of reach of a verifier. The functional properties of asynchronous copies, TMA, producer-consumer pipelines and the barriers coordinating them have not been formalized, especially the corner cases that arise when using these synchronization constructs. Modeling each new construct as it arrives has not kept pace with the hardware. However, verification tools do work on much simpler programs, so RESOLVE reduces the kernel to one of those.

Reduction runs on a candidate that passed determinism testing (§3) and whose output differs from the reference. When their outputs agree bitwise on every test, RESOLVE stops there: the candidate has been tested to compute a function, and that function matches the reference. Reduction could produce the same program from both sides, and the proof step would add nothing. This is not unusual, since 15 of the 100 pairs in RKB are bitwise identical (§6.2).

An agent is instructed to rewrite each kernel using as little concurrency as possible:

  • •

    Barriers, atomics, cooperative launches and warp primitives are rejected, including inside headers, macros, template expansions and inline PTX.

  • •

    Multiple kernel launches are allowed. Splitting a large fused kernel into several simple ones is usually easier than flattening it into one, since we minimize concurrency and not launches.

  • •

    Repeated statements should become loops and shared code should become functions, since the later proof effort grows with bulk.

Reduction usually reaches a single thread, but not always. The exact floating-point behavior of tensor cores is difficult to model in one thread, especially across data types, and could evolve across architectures. We expect the future to bring more such instructions. Rather than reduce away from them, we allow the least concurrency the instruction requires, which for a tensor core is a single warp, and for the warpgroup instructions on Hopper is four. Modern verification tools such as Kuiper (Martínez et al., 2026) provide semantics for these instructions over the reals, so the reduction can keep them rather than imitate them. The floor is set by the instruction, which is why the rule is as little concurrency as possible and not a single thread.

A reduction is accepted only if it reproduces the output of the original, bitwise, on every tested input. There is no tolerance, no epsilon and no normalization in this comparison. We have found modern agents, with the testing tooling available to them, very capable of producing reductions that pass. The result is now a simplified program that a verifier can reasonably handle.

5. Proof

After reduction, we are left with two simple programs, each bitwise equal to the original kernel they replace. Yet, their outputs still differ from each other. Such a difference may be benign and not indicative of a bug: algebraically sound changes like reassociating a reduction, distributing a product over a sum, or using fused-multiply-add instruction instead of doing the operations individually can change rounding behavior when using floating point numbers, and cause low-order bits to differ. In practice, many such rewrites are routinely done by programmers when they believe they can increase performance, as long as some final numerical error check stays within bounds. This is unsatisfactory since there is no principled way to define acceptable error, or which of the two programs is more correct than the other (without using a higher-precision reference). We rely on testing too, but only for bitwise equality. The problem is the tolerance, not the testing: someone has to choose it, and that choice decides which bugs stay visible.

In our approach, we aim to prove that the programs satisfy a common algebraic specification, where numerical error is ignored, and one can only reason symbolically about the result. That is, we do not intend to prove that the outputs on each side are “close enough” (in fact we do not even want to define what such a thing would mean) but instead prove, formally, that they both morally compute the same algebraic expression and, that if the precision of floats was infinite, they would match exactly and compute the exact same real number.

This approach was introduced by Kuiper (Martínez et al., 2026), where the authors introduce an abstract “approximation” relation (≈\approx) between floating point numbers of any precision and real numbers. The relation can only be introduced for literals, and is preserved by the basic arithmetic operations (i.e. x≈r∧y≈sx\approx r\wedge y\approx s implies x+y≈r+sx+y\approx r+s, where the first ++ is floating-point addition and the second one is real addition). Mathematical library functions, like square root and exponentiation, get similar assumptions. This relation decouples reasoning about the floating point numbers and the reals they are meant to compute, such that while there is no way to prove that f+(g+h)f+(g+h) equals (f+g)+h(f+g)+h (this would be unsound, as they can differ), it can instead be proven that they both approximate x+y+zx+y+z, with xx, yy, zz reals such that f≈x∧g≈y∧h≈zf\approx x\wedge g\approx y\wedge h\approx z, since, in the reals, (x+y)+z(x+y)+z is equal to x+(y+z)x+(y+z). This decoupling allows to give families of algorithms (e.g. GEMMs) that make different low-level choices (due to tiling, intrinsics, use of tensor cores, etc) a common simple top-level specification (e.g. the output approximates the real matrix product).

This last feature, proving two bitwise-inequivalent programs satisfy a same approximate specification, is the one we rely on for the last stage of RESOLVE. For each reduced kernel, we find Kuiper implementations that are bit-equivalent to each. This connection is also established via testing, after the Kuiper program is extracted and built. Then, coding agents prove that the two Kuiper programs a share a common functional approximate specification, ensuring they perform the same algebraic computation. Figure 4 shows how these links connect the original kernels to that specification.

To be effective at this process, it is useful to have a corpus of verified kernels to refer to. Martínez and Sorensen (2026) have already obtained verified solutions to all of KernelBench level 1 challenges, and have audited the specifications for quality to ensure, e.g., that they are not trivially satisfiable. The agents we used during this procedure were pointed to this public dataset and also to a growing database of kernel we had already verified.

The verification process can fail when the programs are in fact not equivalent. In this case, the failing proof usually makes it clear where the problem is, and coding agents can, in our experience, explain this in simple terms. An interesting failure mode occurs when the programs output values that are close, but that cannot be related via the approximation relation of Kuiper. Take for instance a program computing exe^{x} using a Taylor series approximation of degree 10, and one of degree 11. While for all practical purposes these two could be “close enough” and a precise error bound could be proven, the idealized real reasoning of Kuiper does not allow to prove these equivalent. In the reals, both sides are simply different. Optimizations of this sort do show up in GPU kernel optimization, and RESOLVE currently rejects them. It is interesting future work to account for these by providing concrete error budgets or similar.

There is a crucial component here: the specification SS must be tight, i.e., even if using the approximation relation, the real numbers on the RHS must be precisely defined. In other words, SS should state that the output is a function of the inputs over the reals. It is possible in Kuiper, as in many verification tools, to give a weak specification that only guarantees that the program is safe, but no particular functional postcondition. If this is so, then the fact that two programs share a common specification does not say much about their relative behaviors. We ask the agents to construct tight specifications only, and validate this with some human review. An automated method to certify that specifications are tight would be useful here, and we leave it to future work.

After a successful run, three facts now hold for each side:

  • •

    the kernel is bitwise equal to its reduced program;

  • •

    the reduced program is bitwise equal to the verified program;

  • •

    the verified program satisfies the common, tight specification SS.

Both sides therefore satisfy the same specification, so the candidate computes the function the reference defines, even though the bits differ.

6. Evaluation

We evaluate RESOLVE on three sets of kernels, each fused more aggressively than the last, ending with production mega-kernels where it exposes real bugs and validates the agent-written fixes.

  1. (§6.2)

    On the KernelBench corpus (Ouyang et al., 2025) we demonstrate how RESOLVE operates on a breadth of simple kernels of the kind agents are commonly asked to optimize. We perform a mutation study to explore how hard concurrency errors are to catch, and we reduce and prove a subset of the corpus.

  2. (§6.3)

    We examine three implementations of a fused MLP kernel, critical to modern LLM implementations, spanning three widely used performance-oriented languages: CUTLASS, Gluon and Triton. For all three kernels we test, reduce and prove the optimized variant against a PyTorch reference.

  3. (§6.4)

    We turn to mega-kernels, which fuse wider spans of a model into a single launch. The determinism tester exposes bugs in several of them, along with other behavior that diverges significantly from their reference implementations, and for two we show an agent repairing the kernel with the fix tested by RESOLVE.

The RESOLVE stages vary in how much time and tokens they consume. The determinism tester is cheap: it samples rather than tracing everything, prunes the scopes where a kernel can have no conflict, and works on the compiled binary. That leaves it fast enough to run in a tight loop, or inside a full application wherever a deterministic output can be logged and checked (§6.4). Reduction, specification and proof are agent tasks and are much slower and more costly. In our context, this is acceptable, given that the primary goal of RESOLVE is to validate kernels as part of a larger automatic optimization system which can run without human interaction, not an interactive tool for hunting bugs.

6.1. Setup

All experiments run on a server with four NVIDIA H100 PCIe GPUs, sm_90 with CUDA 13.0, hosted on an AMD EPYC 9554 running Linux 6.8. Independent jobs take one GPU each, and no two experiments share a GPU. Agents appear throughout. They perform the reductions, write the specifications, write the Kuiper programs and check that each one reproduces the execution it stands for, along with tasks particular to each experiment, such as mutant generation in §6.2 and kernel repair in §6.4. Every agent runs through the Copilot CLI with reasoning effort set to max, on GPT-5.6.

Our corpus is not rich enough to calibrate the determinism tester empirically, so we use settings that pilot experiments found practical: four unperturbed runs, delays of up to 5,000 cycles inserted with probability 0.8, a 200-million-record memory tracing cap, and eight randomly chosen CTAs for both tracing and perturbation. Section 6.2 shows that cap is large enough to identify the memory regions and scopes worth testing. Baselines are written in PyTorch and executed in eager mode. We assume they are deterministic, which informal runs of our determinism tester corroborate. All system and GPU calls are checked for errors.

6.2. KernelBench Level 1

To establish how well RESOLVE works across the kinds of kernels agents are frequently asked to optimize, we begin with a study over KernelBench Level 1 (Ouyang et al., 2025). We ask two questions: can the RESOLVE pipeline validate the kernels in this suite, and when a kernel contains a bug, does RESOLVE catch it?

Validating kernels.

Recall from §2.1 that RKB pairs each KernelBench Level 1 kernel with an optimized candidate, and that each kernel comes with a set of input distributions. Our first test over them is cheap: we run the kernel executor and compare output hashes. 15 of the 100 candidates can be classified after running just the determinism tester. For the remaining 85 we draw two samples from each input distribution, and carry 14 of them through the full workflow, which keeps the study tractable.

The top of Table 1 summarizes the outcomes observed for the 17 kernels that could be classified by just the determinism tester. 15 were found to be deterministic and bitwise equivalent. Two, however, were detected to perform no memory accesses at all and were thus flagged by RESOLVE as incorrect. Specifically, for problems 31 and 32, an elementwise ELU and a hardtanh, the agent had erroneously produced an empty kernel that does no computation. We cannot say why, whether it failed silently or judged its task complete too early. Both nonetheless pass the tolerance tests KernelBench ships with, supporting our earlier claim that tolerance-based validation is susceptible to false negatives. Prior work has argued that an incorrect kernel can pass such thresholds (Martínez and Sorensen, 2026); these cases show an agent producing them and a real-world tolerance suite accepting them.

The bottom of Table 1 summarizes the outcomes for the kernels that required running the full RESOLVE workflow. Eleven of the 14 came through. For each, the agents reduced both programs, wrote a specification, and produced Kuiper programs verified against it and bitwise equivalent to the kernels they stand for. Just to be sure, we inspected every specification by hand and found each one to be tight.

Two of the three that did not complete the verification share a cause. Each reaches for inline PTX to get a fast approximation or an explicit rounding mode that Kuiper has no wrapper for: one substitutes inline assembly for exp and log1p and flushes subnormals to zero, and another does the same for SELU. Wrapping thread-local operations of this kind is routine, of the sort that added __expf above, and nothing like the effort of formalizing a concurrency construct.

The third is more interesting: A sigmoid candidate replaces the exponential with a Taylor approximation, which is not algebraically equivalent to the reference. Thus our tool "correctly" failed to prove equivalence. However, this does not mean the kernel is buggy. Rather, correctness of an approximating kernel simply cannot be determined without reasoning about numerical tolerance, of the kind developed for floating-point expressions on CPUs (Panchekha et al., 2015), which our approach does not do and which we leave to future work.

Table 2 reports what each stage cost. Specification and proof dominate both: they take four times as long as reduction and consume more than a hundred times the tokens. Almost all of that is input. The agent reads about eighty-five tokens for every one it writes, because each attempt at a proof re-reads the context and returns a small edit. Supporting these kernels required adding __expf to Kuiper, which already had expf and takes the same specification, an approximation of the exponential over the reals. We expect further thread-local semantics to be needed as RESOLVE is applied more widely.

Catching synchronization bugs.

Next we investigate how RESOLVE’s determinism tester fares on kernels containing synchronization errors. In particular, we were interested to see how many and what type of synchronization errors manifest as nondeterminism and subsequently get flagged. We first build a suite called RKB-Mutant by instructing an agent to inject a single synchronization fault into each RKB candidate, using four mutators in two groups.

  • •

    Synchronization removed, moved, or weakened. A barrier or asynchronous wait is deleted, swapped with the memory access that follows it, or narrowed in scope from cluster to block or block to warp.

  • •

    Write destinations aliased. Distinct per-thread destinations are mapped onto one, so threads that never conflicted now write the same location.

Applying every mutator to every kernel gives 400 attempts, which we filter in two stages. An agent critic discards the attempts where the mutator had no site to apply to, such as a kernel with no barrier to remove or no shared destination to alias, which accounts for 202. Of the 198 that remain, a further 55 fail to run and are excluded. This leaves 143 mutant kernels.

The determinism tester flagged 92 of the 143 synchronization mutants. Testing one took 405 seconds on average, ranging from 88 to 4,587. A catch costs less than a clean run, because the tester stops at the first mismatch: the 92 it caught averaged 256 seconds and none took longer than 1,091.

We reviewed all 51 misses with the help of an agent, and they fall into three groups. Three are mutants injected into code that never runs, so there is no fault to catch. Twenty-eight introduce a race that never changes the value the kernel finally writes. The mutated kernel is still deterministic, which is the property RESOLVE checks, so it has nothing to report, and these 28 are exactly the case §3 makes when it separates a data race from a nondeterministic result.

The remaining 20 place their conflict inside a single warp, where no delay we can insert will separate two threads and we know of no perturbation an NVBit-based tool could apply to expose them. Every mutant that made a kernel nondeterministic and lay within reach of binary instrumentation was caught. Reaching inside the warp needs compiler support or a static analysis, and is future work. Per-mutant results are given in the artifact.

Of the 92 we catch, 90 mismatch across repeated runs with no perturbation at all. Only two need a delay to expose them.

Two cases are too few to calibrate a delay policy on, so we do not attempt it here. That does not mean delays are unnecessary: two of the mega-kernel cases in §6.4 are exposed only under perturbation, and prior work reports the same (Stephenson et al., 2026). It is the KernelBench mutants that do not need them, because an injected synchronization fault usually makes the kernel visibly nondeterministic. We swept the delay length from 1,000 to 20,000 cycles, doubling at each step, and the probability from 0.25 to 1 in steps of 0.25; both mutants that need a delay were detected at every setting.

Even where perturbation is not required, the tracing pass still has a budget, and we can measure both what it costs and how many potential conflicts it finds. Figure 5 sweeps that budget from one million records to four hundred million. Below 100 million the trace saturates on the larger kernels and loses conflicts entirely: at 50 million the inter-block indicator disappears. At 100 million every case traces to completion, and the conflict inventory is unchanged at 200 and 400 million while the mean time to configure a kernel rises from 107 to 153 seconds. We trace 200 million records, one step past the point where the inventory stops changing. Two CTAs were enough to find every conflict indicator on this suite, and two is the fewest that can expose a conflict between CTAs at all. That nothing further appears beyond two is evidence for the assumption in §3.1 that CTAs are largely interchangeable.

6.3. A Fused MLP Kernel

The kernel fuses the up projection, the gate projection and the SwiGLU activation of an MLP block, the arrangement used by current models such as Qwen. Written the usual way this is three kernels, and the two projections must write their results to memory for the activation to read them back. Fusing the three removes four passes over those intermediates and makes the block run up to 2.5×2.5\times faster than the PyTorch implementation of the same block. Neither PyTorch’s compiler nor TensorRT performs the fusion, because it has to cross two projections that use different weight matrices. At the time of writing, no compiler will automatically produce this kernel.

Our reference is PyTorch in eager mode, where the three operations run as three kernels. Against it we place three aggressively optimized variants, one each in Triton (Tillet et al., 2019), Gluon (Triton Contributors, 2026) and CUTLASS (NVIDIA, 2023), each fusing the work into a single kernel and each written with the help of an agent. They are the fastest implementations of this operation we are aware of. We validate them at a representative size, a hidden dimension of 8,192 and an FFN intermediate size of 29,568 against 4,096 rows of activations. None of the three matches the reference bitwise, because the fusion reorders the reductions, and all three are intricate enough that correctness cannot be taken for granted. Gluon and Triton do match each other bitwise, so we carried only Gluon through specification and proof.

As far as we are aware, these kernels are out of reach for existing rigorous validation, on both halves of the problem. For concurrency, Compute Sanitizer (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026) runs on all three and reports nothing, which is the answer we expect and also all it can offer: a clean race report says neither that the kernel is deterministic nor that it computes the reference function. SuperCollider (Stephenson et al., 2026) reaches individual accesses through a CUDA compiler pass, which two of our three variants cannot go through because they are not written in CUDA. For functional correctness, the kernels are built out of asynchronous memory copies and tensor core instructions, which verification tools such as ProofWright (Chatterjee et al., 2026) do not model.

RESOLVE establishes the equivalence of all three variants against the PyTorch reference. Table 3 reports what each one took. Reduction and proof both run faster than the RKB medians in Table 2, even though these kernels are far more intricate, because matrix multiplication was studied heavily in the work that produced Kuiper (Martínez et al., 2026) and the corpus an agent can draw on is correspondingly rich for kernels of this shape. Determinism testing runs the other way and takes several times longer, because these kernels run at the sizes a deployed model uses rather than benchmark sizes, leaving far more memory traffic to trace.

New languages and compilers for writing this kind of code keep appearing (NVIDIA, 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Soi et al., 2026), and which one produces the fastest kernel for a given operation keeps changing as they develop. An agent optimizing a kernel should be able to move it from any one of these languages to another and still know it computes the same function, which is what RESOLVE gives it.

6.4. Mega-Kernels

A mega-kernel takes fusion further again. Where §6.3 fuses three operations into one kernel, these fuse much wider spans of a model, and they are the most aggressively fused GPU code we know of. We ran RESOLVE over three of them, each in its single-GPU configuration.

  • •

    LUCE (Ciffa, 2026) fuses all 24 decoder layers of a hybrid DeltaNet and attention model into a single launch.

  • •

    FlashMoE (Aimuyo et al., 2025) fuses the routing and expert dispatch of a mixture-of-experts layer.

  • •

    FastMoE (He et al., 2021) provides a native capacity-pruning kernel for mixture-of-experts routing.

We also attempted Mirage (Cheng et al., 2025), which compiles a model into a persistent mega-kernel. It hung when run under our determinism tester and we could not diagnose why, so we report nothing for it. Per-system configurations are given in the artifact.

Testing mega-kernels.

These kernels differ from everything above in one practical respect: they do not come with kernel executors. Each is embedded in a larger framework and is exercised only through that framework’s own tests. Our first pass therefore runs the determinism tester over those existing test suites, with an agent identifying outputs that should be deterministic and logging them at each stage of the pipeline.

That the determinism tester can be pointed at code in this shape is a consequence of working at the binary. It is at its most convenient given a kernel executor, but NVBit will instrument nearly any NVIDIA binary, so the requirement reduces to identifying an output that should not change between runs and logging it. Nothing about the framework around the kernel has to be understood.

What each run exercises, and what was logged from it:

  • •

    LUCE: a full decode step of Qwen3.5-0.8B. Logged: the generated token and the final hidden state.

  • •

    FlashMoE: the router alone, with the experts overloaded so the capacity limit binds. Logged: expert demand, and the surviving tokens and their probabilities.

  • •

    FastMoE: the capacity-pruning kernel, on assignments that exceed capacity. Logged: the pruned experts and the survival mask.

Nondeterministic outputs.

All three mega-kernels behaved nondeterministically. An agent could then work on each one with the determinism tester in hand, guessing at a cause, re-running the tester to check the guess, and narrowing the search by delta debugging (Zeller and Hildebrandt, 2002). Four root causes came out: two in LUCE, one in FlashMoE and one in FastMoE.

LUCE’s two are plainly bugs. In the grid barrier, block 0 resets the arrival counters while other blocks may already be arriving, and __syncthreads() cannot order one block against another. The blog post that introduces the kernel mentions hitting grid synchronization problems during development (Ciffa, 2026), so a barrier problem is not a complete surprise. The second one looks unknown: several attention blocks write the same global scratch buffer, because the address they compute for it carries no block or head offset, and nothing we found mentions it. The barrier was also the only one that showed up reliably without perturbation. The other three needed inserted delays before they appeared consistently.

The two routing causes are harder to classify. Both come from capacity. When an expert fills, routed tokens are dropped, and in both systems the tokens that get dropped depend on the order blocks arrive: FlashMoE reserves slots with atomics, and FastMoE prunes with atomicSub. Every reference implementation we know of routes deterministically and drops the same set of tokens once capacity binds. These two do not, and neither paper says so. Whether that should be treated as a bug is under discussion.

Fixing the bugs.

We asked the agents to repair each root cause. A kernel counted as fixed once it ran under the determinism tester without any nondeterminism showing up, which is a weaker bar than the rest of this paper uses. Table 4 gives what each repair changed and what it cost in performance. The two LUCE repairs came out marginally faster than the code they replaced, which we read as noise rather than a win. FlashMoE’s costs under a percent, so there is no performance argument for leaving its router nondeterministic. FastMoE is the one case where determinism is not close to free, at ten percent, and that is the case where whether the behavior is a bug is worth a discussion.

We then attempted the whole pipeline on each fixed kernel, writing a straightforward PyTorch reference out of the operators the system implements. FastMoE came out bitwise identical to its reference, so nothing further was needed. FlashMoE did not. We reduced it in 25 minutes, but could not specify it in Kuiper, which has no support for argmax. The router picks experts with one, and an argmax returns an index rather than a real and is discontinuous at ties, so the approximation relation of §5 does not carry across it. Specifying the capacity stage on its own, taking the assignments as input, avoids the argmax, and we leave this to future work. LUCE we could not reduce at all: its matrix multiplies use the Hopper warpgroup instructions, whose floor is 128 threads, and our reducer handles nothing above a single warp. Raising that floor means extending the reducer, and extending Kuiper with those semantics as well.

We are working on reporting each of these upstream, along with the fix we recommend.

7. Related Work

Determinism and race freedom.

Data-race freedom buys a simpler model to reason in, since a program without races behaves as though the machine were sequentially consistent (Adve and Hill, 1990). Determinism buys something similar and has its own history, going back to determinacy races in Cilk (Feng and Leiserson, 1997) and to runtime checks that a program’s output does not depend on the schedule (Burnim and Sen, 2009). Type systems can guarantee determinism statically, on the CPU (Bocchino et al., 2009) and on the GPU (Köpcke et al., 2023).

Lipton reduction merges statements into coarser atomic blocks (Lipton, 1975; Elmas et al., 2009). Sequentialization goes further and emits an equivalent sequential program (Lal and Reps, 2008; Inverso et al., 2014). These are complete guarantees, but require source code to be available. By contrast, we run the binary under perturbation and watch the output; §6.2 lists the mutants that slip past. However our approach scales to binary kernel compiled from in Gluon or CUTLASS.

Verified optimizers.

Tools like CompCert and Exo provide general correctness guarantees, one by verifying the compiler (Leroy, 2006) and the other by building schedules only out of transformations already known to preserve semantics (Ikarashi et al., 2022).

A long line of work checks that the output of the optimizer is equivalent to its input for each particular run, instead of trusting or verifying the tool. Translation validation checks a single compilation instead of the compiler (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000). Alive2 takes two LLVM functions and determines refinement by encoding the problem to SMT (Lopes et al., 2021). This approach has also been used in superoptimizers to ensure correctness (Schkufza et al., 2013). For tensor programs the same problem appears as graph substitutions, either verified up front (Jia et al., 2019) or allowed to be wrong and patched afterwards (Wang et al., 2021).

RESOLVE by contrast takes an even more radical approach: not only do we check each problem individually, we also pick a separate notion of equivalence for each problem (by deriving a natural spec that both programs are verified against).

GPU semantics.

Formal models of GPU behavior tend to show up well after the hardware. A first memory consistency model was pinned down empirically in 2015 (Alglave et al., 2015). NVIDIA published a formal one four years after that (Lustig et al., 2019). Testing hardware against such models at scale still finds violations (Levine et al., 2023). Execution inside a warp has no official model, only a proposed operational semantics (Chen et al., 2026). Forward progress between workgroups is undefined, and the candidate models had to be run on real hardware to see which ones held (Sorensen et al., 2021). Named barriers got a model built to verify them (Sharma et al., 2015). Tensor core arithmetic has an SMT formalization, though not from NVIDIA (Valpey et al., 2025). Scoped data-race freedom is a cleaner foundation (Hower et al., 2014), but it only covers programs that respect the scopes, which an aggressively tuned kernel may not.

None of this blocks RESOLVE’s determinism tester, since it does not require a formal model of each hardware feature. It only tests the general property that how long a memory access takes should not change the semantics of a program. Therefore we can verify kernels that use named barriers without even needing to know what named barriers are, let alone have a correct and practically usable formal semantics for them. Kuiper however still requires semantics for features that are used in the sequentialized kernels, and that blocks two kernels using certain thread-local operations (§6.2).

8. Conclusion

RESOLVE combines testing, reduction, and proof to validate optimized GPU kernels across languages and frameworks. Our evaluation evaluated 31 KernelBench Level 1 kernels, three fused MLP implementations in CUTLASS, Triton, and Gluon against a common PyTorch reference, and a mixture-of-experts kernel from an existing system. The determinism tester also caught 92 injected synchronization faults and exposed four previously unreported issues in production mega-kernels, including two clear bugs. These results show that the approach can both uncover errors in deployed code and support validation of optimizations beyond the verifier’s direct semantic coverage. As agents take on more of kernel development, they need validation they can trust, enough detail to debug what fails, and the freedom to write in whatever language is fastest at the time.

Acknowledgments

Agents were used widely throughout this work. They wrote and optimized kernels, performed the reductions, drafted specifications and Kuiper proofs, and proposed the repairs. The text of this paper was organized and drafted by people, and agents polished and reviewed it. The project itself was directed by people. The scientific arguments, the validation of every result reported here, and the integrity of the artifact are ours. The agents ran through GitHub Copilot CLI, which lets the underlying model be configured; most of this work used GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
